utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the appearances?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am Eric Ostberg, appearing today with Ms. Teresa McHenry, Mr. Giuliano Turone, Mr. Stefan Waespi and our case manager, Elles van Dusschoten. Thank you. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. My name is Edina Residovic, defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-defendant (sic) is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor from Canada. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Zeljko Olujic, defence counsel for Mucic. With me in the court is Mr. Michael Greaves, defence attorney from London. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): Good morning, your Honours. I am Salih Karabdic, attorney from Sarajevo, defence counsel for Mr. Hazim Delic. With me in the team is Mr. Tom Moran, attorney from Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours. I am John Ackerman, appearing for Mr. Esad Landzo. Ms McMurrey is due to return today. Probably she is between Schipol Airport and here and may even appear in this very court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is the defence now satisfied with the exhibits they were to look at yesterday? Yes, Mr. Olujic, are you now satisfied with the exhibits? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, we received yesterday after our request the tapes which were viewed this morning, but we have still not received the transcript as the Prosecution has promise to supply. MS. RESIDOVIC (in interpretation): Your Honours, the same applies to us. We have received the video recordings, which is about one to one and a half hours long. We haven't received the transcript, which we consider to be important for the cross-examination of the witness we heard yesterday, so that we can continue the cross-examination. MR. KARABDIC (in interpretation): I should also like to declare, like my colleagues, that I have received the videotapes, but not the transcript, and I feel that it is not possible to continue cross-examination without the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostberg? What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: The Office of the Prosecutor is busily trying to provide the defence with this transcript and it's in progress and will be ready during this day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think you are satisfied with this assurance. We can continue. The idea was to continue with the other witnesses until the transcripts are supplied and then you can go on with cross-examination. I know there are some reservations about the possibility of the contents of the transcripts being available and helpful, but I suppose these are quite different witnesses and we can go on with them. Can we have a witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. The next witness will be Mr. Johannes Gschwendt. (Witness enters court) (Interpreter enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Gentlemen, because of the difficulty in spacing the booths, there is a German interpreter who can interpret directly to this witness. MR. JOHANNES GSCHEWENDT (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please swear the interpreter. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): I beg your pardon, your Honours. Could the interpreter please introduce herself, so that we know who she is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please swear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Good morning. Should I introduce myself now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Swear to the oath first. Swear. (Interpreter sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What is your name? Introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: My name is Gabriella Konig. I am here as the interpreter from English into German for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please I will advise counsel to know how to organise themselves. It is not right to behave the way Mr. Olujic has done. Now I think it is safer to read in German Rule 76 for her. You are not a witness. The oath you are swearing is not a witness' oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The interpreter should translate faithfully whatever the witness states.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I swear that I will faithfully translate everything the witness says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Sit down. You can both sit down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I now proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Johannes Gschwendt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 9th September 1961.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I think I have to be rather slow waiting for the translation into Serbo-Croatian; is that correct? So, Mr. Gschwendt, which is your citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am an Austrian national.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am a supervising police officer in Austria.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say exactly which position you have now inside the Austrian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am at present with the EDOC -- that's the unit -- to fight against organised crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Which degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have the same position in March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, March 1996 I didn't have that title and I wasn't in the same position at the time. I was working with the Vienna Police Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: With which degree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was First Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In which year did you get the position you had in March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1st January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt, can you please describe briefly your professional curriculum, starting from the type of school you attended?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1980 I went to police school, as it's called, for two years, and for four years I was a police officer. Then for one year I was in a course, followed a course for detectives, and then for five years I was a detective. Then for two years I followed an officer's course, as it's called, and since 1st January 1993 I'm a senior police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Gschwendt, coming back to your position you had until last month, and you had in March 1996, where are the premises of the 1st Division located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 1st District of Vienna, Schottenring, Schottenring 7-9, 3rd floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In your official capacity you had in 1996, do you usually carry on criminal investigations on particular crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, especially state police matters, in other words, terrorism, proliferation (sic), arms dealings, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Before this present occasion did you have other occasion to testify in court as a result of your investigative work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have testified in court several times, but not in connection with international trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Gschwendt, are you aware of a request of cooperation signed by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal and directed to the Austrian authorities for the arrest of Mr. Zdravko Mucic and Mr. Zejnil Delalic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. 13th March 1996 was when I learned of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did that request also concern the fulfillment of how searches or seizures related to the same proceedings of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that was two days later that that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean, the request done by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, did that concern also the fulfillment of seizures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Tribunal, asked for provisional measures against Zejnil Delalic and Zdravko Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you take part in the police operations concerning all this and in which role, which function?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I did participate, yes, and my role was the operational measures, to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say more precisely what were your duties as Operational Manager and Operational Officer, as Chief Operational Officer, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Well, it was my job to see to it that the arrests were carried out and that the searches were carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean you took charge of the general organisation of the operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did these police operations take place in cooperation with Interpol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was cooperation with Interpol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there a time when you met with some Interpol officer in order to prepare these police operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a discussion in the Federal Ministry of the Interior and there was on-going telephone contact.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately when these contacts happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Second week of March, in the course of that week.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When were you informed, I mean informed in some detail, about the charges raised by the Prosecutor of this Tribunal against Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 13th March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How did you get this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In written form? You mean on which document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on a document -- in writing. This document apparently had been sent to Interpol and Interpol passed it on to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean the request of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did the Austrian judge issue the arrest warrants and the search warrants concerning Mr. Delalic and Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrests -- 14th March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Both arrest warrants and search warrants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The search warrants on 15th March were adjusted, that is to say two addresses were added to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say the name of the judge who issued these warrants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Investigating judge Dr Peter Seda.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say how many places were supposed to be searched according to the warrant?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether there were six search warrants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say in particular which places were supposed to be searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was the apartment of Zdravko Mucic, Taubergasse 15, Door 10. Then an apartment of the MAS company, which we reckoned was Zejnil Delalic's. That is Taubergasse 15, Door 14. Then Taubergasse 15 on the ground floor was where there's the BIH Bosnian Club and the office of the MAS company. Then Taubergasse 28, that's the house opposite, and that was where the MAS company had its work rooms. Koppstrasse 14, 1, 5, 6 and 7, that is INDA-BAU Company. At the time there was a sign up saying that these rooms or facilities were also used by the MAS company, and Hasnerstrasse 32, 27 and 29 there. That's the apartment of Djemal Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt, how were the plans with regard to the arrest of Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plans at the time were that Zdravko Mucic and Zejnil Delalic would be arrested at the same time so that there can't be any contacts between them and initially this was scheduled for 19th March 1996. Mucic was in Vienna and Delalic was in Germany and on the basis of what the German colleagues told us the arrest took place on 18th March.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: How was the arrest of Mr. Mucic carried on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic had been under observation and when we were informed that the German colleagues were going to be taking action, I said -- I gave the order, as it were, that our people should also take action, and Mr. Mucic at that point in time was in the street in Natagasse (sic) and at 2.15 pm he was arrested by four officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When did you personally learn about the completion of the arrest of Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About a minute later at most by radio.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: From whom did you learn that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From Panzer, who was there at the site of the arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt, was there any investigator of this Tribunal present at the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Had the Prosecuting Office of this Tribunal requested that any of its investigators be present at the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean, "not to me"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not personally to me, to the Interpol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you. Approximately at what time did you see Mr. Mucic the first time that day? We are talking about March 18th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 5.00 pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 3rd floor, Schottenring 7-9, in our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What do you mean Schottenring 7-9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Schottenring. That's the address.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sorry. That's in the police premises. Can you say in which room exactly in the police premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there's two rooms that are side by side, 331 and 329.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What was the room in which Mr. Mucic was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who was with you, Mr. Gschwendt, when you first saw Mr. Mucic in Room 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Moerbauer, Panzer, Mr. Borlak and Ms. Supput, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So did Mr. Borlak, Moerbauer, Panzer arrive together with Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At that minute you were in Room 331 together with Ms. Supput, the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you say anything to Mr. Mucic at this point as soon as he arrived with the help of the interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did somebody else tell Mr. Mucic about his rights at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was informed of his rights several times and when he was brought to the police premises he was informed of his rights as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Yes. Can you give us some details about this giving him information about his right as soon as he arrived at the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we have some forms. One of them is the information sheet for arrested persons and there the information is spelled out. The second item is the custody report and it's customary for us to inform people of their rights such that they are told that they need not incriminate themselves, that they need not speak, that if they are foreigners, as was the case with Mucic, they may notify their Embassy, and that they may notify a lawyer or a person of their confidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who did personally explain all this to Mr. Mucic right after his arrival at the police headquarters in your presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was explained to him by Ms. Supput, the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did she explain the entire content of this information sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. She translated that information sheet and read it out to Mr. Mucic in his native tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Could you say more precisely what was said to him, to Mr. Mucic, about his right to be assisted by a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he was told that he could contact a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic say anything at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was quite calm and at the outset he talked but little.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic sign any document on receipt of this informations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic signed the custody report and thereby he confirmed that he was acquainted with the information sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic want, request, to contact a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not, and at the end of the it was brought to his attention that he would be questioned by the investigating judge on the following day and with a view to preparation he was once again asked whether he wanted a lawyer and I believe that his last statement, in fact, was that at that point in time he did not need a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Going back to the sheet of information on which Mr. Mucic put his signature, does his answer concerning the request to have a lawyer appear on this sheet, information sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the custody report, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did he sign anything about the possibility of calling a defence lawyer immediately as soon as he arrived at the police headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That question is in the custody report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: And he answered "no", you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic remain in Room 331 after this initial appearance in that room and after giving him this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whether he was there the whole time I can't say, because I was dealing with other organisational matters, but he was there originally and then at 1.30 in the morning when he was handed over to a court that is where he was taken from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Mucic ever remain alone in Room 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For security reasons that was out of the question. There were always at least two to three officers with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt, did you see in this same day of March 18th any investigator or any officer of this Tribunal, the prosecuting office of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Subsequently I think there were three people from the Tribunal who were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Present where?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the police headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: You mean in Room 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Room 331 as well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Approximately at what time did they arrive in Room 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I mean very approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you see any of them having any conversation with Mr. Mucic? Did any of them ask you to talk to Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Then can you describe, as far as you can remember, and in detail as far as you can remember, this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot any more. I don't remember. I simply can't reconstruct it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But was that one person or more than one person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several people, two to three people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you remember that a conversation occurred in your presence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: But did this conversation take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It took place, but I can no longer describe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Simply because you have forgotten it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately how long did the ICTY officers remain in the police headquarters that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say with any provision, because they were there several times. They were there the following day as well, and no record was kept of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to see the ICTY officers again that day of March 18th or in the following days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw them on the following day as well and on 17th as well. That's the day before, when they arrived in Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: What did on the 17th occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 17th the people from the Tribunal arrived and I sent two men to the airport to get in touch with the people from the Tribunal and apparently that didn't quite work out and late in the evening, around 11 o'clock, I got a call on my mobile telephone and I went to see the Tribunal people at their hotel to do what was necessary in respect of the contacts for the coming days with Interpol, etc.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Let us go now to the police interview with Mr. Mucic which took place in the evening of March 18th. Did the interview take place in Room 331?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you take part in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part I did. I couldn't participate throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Were you present when the interview started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the beginning, yes. Mr. Borlak informed Mr. Mucic of his rights via the interpreter and asked him for his personal particulars, and then we always begin this kind of an interview with information about the individual, just some bio data about the individual in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: At this very stage, I mean at the beginning of the interview, which were the rights Mr. Mucic was informed about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was informed firstly of his right to consult a lawyer and that he did not -- there was no need for him to incriminate himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt, at any time prior to the interview did Mr. Mucic ever suggest that he might wish to consult an attorney?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not. He did also not request a lawyer for the following day, as you can see on the last page of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Sir, did you or anyone else ever suggest to Mr. Mucic any reason for which he should not consult an attorney for any reason?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This would not have made any sense for us to say such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say what languages were used during the interview, the police interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The officers spoke German and the interpreter spoke German and Serbo-Croatian. The language is Serbo-Croatian but I don't speak Serbo-Croatian myself. Mr. Mucic spoke Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was anything said to Mr. Mucic in an effort to induce him to speak to the Austrian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nein.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I didn't get the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said "nein".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Nein. Was anything promised to Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nothing was promised to Mr. Mucic. We were unable to promise him anything, because we had no influence on what would happen subsequently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Just a minute. I didn't say "nine". I said "nein". That is what he said. He said "nein."

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Nein in German, N-E-I-N, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It was "nein".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Was that the answer to the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The previous question the witness said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am just pointing out the correction in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In the end no pressure was done on Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was to pressure exerted on Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say who were the persons present in the room during the police interview and who were the persons taking part in the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present partly, but not for the whole time. Mr. Borlak began the questioning and Mr. Moerbauer continued with it. Mr. Panzer and Bycek were present the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Only these two last people were present the whole time? I mean, were all the other people except you present throughout the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say, because I wasn't there myself the whole time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Can you say approximately at what time was the interview finished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time after 1 o'clock in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Was there any break during the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several short breaks. Coffee and Coca-Cola were drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Who were the persons who signed the interview record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The officers who I named beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. I have just a couple of questions more. Mr. Gschwendt, did at any time Mr. Mucic or any of his legal representatives protest against any of the actions or omissions of the Austrian authorities towards him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no protests at all on the part of Mr. Mucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to see Mr. Mucic again in the following days or weeks after the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw him about 1.30 am, on 19th that is, and once he was transferred to the court I did not see him again. I'm seeing him for the first time again now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: When you say 1.30 am, you mean really 1.30 am or 1.30 pm?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: In the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was brought to our detention centre from our headquarters so that he could be transferred to the court because we don't have any premises where we can detain people in our headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: So that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can't detain him overnight. We do have an arrest cell, but it's not a cell -- it's a cell for short-term arrests but it's not a place where we can detain people for any length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. So you are talking about something which happened right after the end of the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Did you have any occasion to see any of the ICTY officers in the following days after the interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the next day they came to our office and they made copies of certain things which they needed for the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Okay. Going back to the times in which the ICTY officers were in Room 331 on March 18th, was there any possibility for them to speak to Mucic without the presence of your personnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. For security reasons this would not have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Mr. Gschwendt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: My last question is: if any of the prosecuting team of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Had somehow threatened or oppressed Mr. Mucic or otherwise acted improperly, would you have taken action?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That would have been my duty, but this did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gschwendt. This is the end of my examination-in-chief, your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Yes, there will be, your Honours. Cross-examination will proceed in this order: first, counsel for Mr. Mucic; second, counsel for Mr. Delic; third, counsel for Mr. Delalic; and, finally, counsel for Mr. Landzo. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Olujic, you can commence your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you, your Honours. Mr. Gschwendt, my name is Zeljko Olujic. I am defence counsel for Mr. Zdravko Mucic. I have several questions for you. Please be so kind as to make your answers as concise as possible so as to avoid wasting time. I take it that you are -- you believe in the justice of the criminal code of Austria, because that is what I believe too, and I think you could be of assistance in the substance of this matter. Let us proceed. Mr. Gschwendt, will you tell us when you received the request of the International Tribunal and when exactly were you informed that you had to carry out this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received this request on 13th March and on 14th March we took the first measures in order to carry out this request in order to prepare the whole of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. Mr. Gschwendt, does that mean you received it on the 13th, but when did the actual Republic of Austria receive this document? Is there some kind of protocol? Could it be that the state of Austria received it before the 13th, or was the request made to the Republic of Austria on the 13th as well, 13th March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I told you that I have received this on 13th March. It must have been in Austria beforehand, because it has to find its way through the different channels. This takes some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Gschwendt, roughly how much time is needed? Is it a matter of three, four, five or more days, do you think, that Austria received it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends on the type of investigation. It sometimes can take longer if it is sent through the normal traditional channels, but if you use modern telecommunications methods, then it is shorter.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So that you do allow for the possibility that this may have taken longer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say. I can't pass any judgment on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Let us go on. When you received the request did you check who Zdravko Mucic was and what his relationship was with the Republic of Austria? What I mean is: was he a refugee working? Was he a black marketeer? Does he have two or three citizenships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: During the whole of the administrative proceedings we, of course, checked out the situation, where he lives, where he works, with the Austrian authorities, if he had any contact with the Austrian authorities. Until then we examined his background, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: When did you actually learn of his address, where he lives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some time between 13th and 16th of March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you immediately learn his nationality and his native tongue, that it was Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only ascertained what language he spoke at the time that he was arrested. He could have spoken German, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In other words, if I understood you well, of course you did not know at the time what his mother tongue was and what was his citizenship?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct. Usually people from the former Yugoslavia speak Serbo-Croatian but there are some areas where other languages are spoken. There are also Austrians who do not speak German. We had an interpreter available before Mr. Mucic was brought to our premises, because we assumed that he would speak Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Precisely that way in those terms, Serbo-Croatian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not a linguist. I'm not in a position to differentiate between Serbian and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very considerable. In the state of Serbia Serbian is spoken and in the Croatian state the official language is Croatian, but let us go on. Mr. Gschwendt, since you were in charge of the operational proceedings, how many police officers were responsible for the actual arrest and the security of the place where the arrest was carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Can you be rather more precise? Exactly four people or more people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said four people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you take an interpreter with you for this operation, this arrest operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not for the arrest. An arrest is a dangerous affair. You can't take an interpreter with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: At the moment of arrest who was the interpreter for Mr. Pavo Mucic? At the moment of arrest did you have an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the arrest in his apartment his daughter translated for him. I think she was about 16 or 17 years old at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did she interpret well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know because I wasn't there. I was at the police headquarters. I commanded this action.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was the daughter -- will you please answer why an official judicial interpreter was not provided for the actual arrest? What is the reason for this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought he said it was a dangerous exercise and he couldn't go with the interpreter. That was what he said. MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you. I withdraw that question. Mr. Gschwendt, according to the law on criminal procedure of Austria, does the suspect have the right to have a presence of a lawyer when his flat is being searched?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not necessarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Was does that mean? Does that mean that there are situations when that is necessary? When is it necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not necessary because the person concerned was present. The person concerned was present, his daughter was present, someone in whom he has confidence, and there were four police officials present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Therefore, in that situation you allege that according to the Austrian law on criminal procedure he is not entitled to the presence of an attorney, if I have understood you well. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. According to the Austrian law on criminal procedure, does the suspect have the right to the presence of an attorney upon his arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have the translation repeated, please? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Does the suspect have such a right to the presence of a defence attorney at the moment of his arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I may be able to answer this question, but this is not -- doesn't make any sense from a technical point of view, because when the police arrest someone, I do not know of any case where the person's lawyer was present. You do not usually arrest someone in the presence of their lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, according to Austrian law does the Austrian police, upon searching the apartment, have to look for witnesses for the search?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a witness present, a female witness, and the person concerned with the arrest was also present. This is sufficient for our legal procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: If a foreigner is being arrested, does there necessarily have to be an interpreter present?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: How can you explain to him then what is being done in his apartment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic received translation from his daughter and I can say that my police officers speak perfect -- sorry -- they told me that the daughter speaks perfect German.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Gschwendt, when Mr. Mucic was transferred to the police station, was he given over there the papers on his arrest and his rights or were those papers, those forms given to him before then? Were they given to him in the police station or before that during the search or rather the arrest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The arrest warrant and the search warrant were given to him outside. The other forms were only given to him, were only able to be given to him at the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were those forms translated into the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By Ms. Supput, by the interpreter. The interpreter was already there when Mr. Mucic arrived in our office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, Mr. Gschwendt, before this operation did you have any special instructions regarding cooperation with representatives of the International Tribunal in The Hague who had come? Did your department or your service give you any special instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My department, no, but the investigating magistrate, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Were the representatives of the International Tribunal informed by you or your officials regarding the Austrian law on procedure with reference to arrest, the search of apartment and all other things related to this operation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not from me personally, but I assume that they were informed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So they knew what the procedure was in the Republic of Austria, or rather the law on criminal procedure, so you assume they must have been familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would be better if you ask these people when they are in the witness box, but I assume that they did know this.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gschwendt, you were acting, if I may say so, in a rather non-routine operation, that is you were arresting a person for war crimes. You were aware of that, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Did you know exactly which crime he was being charged with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was aware that this concerned war crimes in Celebici, but I did not require precise knowledge, because I had an Austrian arrest warrant, which was issued by the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware perhaps of the conventions regulating these matters, the international covenants and conventions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at the time it was quite difficult, because this was the first case of this kind in Vienna, but the international arrest warrant was turned into, as it were, an Austrian arrest warrant by the investigating judge. So I was working on the basis of an Austrian arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And what did that document say? What was -- according to that warrant, what was he being charged with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, paragraph 321 of the Austrian Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with it, so please be kind enough and describe it to us in your own words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm no lawyer. I don't need to describe it. I have a valid Austrian arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But you don't know what is written in the paragraph 321, what is the substance of that criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. He said: "I'm no lawyer". MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Yes, but the witness knows what it says, so I asked him to be kind enough to tell us in his own free words what that paragraph states, as he just said he did know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes. Be nice enough to tell us what you know about that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Genocide, war crimes and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Does that satisfy you? MR. OLUJIC (in interpretation): Thank you. Thank you. Will you tell me, Mr. Gschwendt, please, for how long was Mr. Mucic interrogated by the police in terms of hours? How many hours, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the rules prevailing in the prison where Mr. Mucic was detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't even know which prison held him. After he was questioned at 1.30 in the morning he was transferred to the Police Detention Centre. As to what prison he was taken to, I don't even know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But the cell that Mr. Zdravko Mucic was held in, was he alone? Was it solitary detention, or were there other people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I wasn't there. Our knowledge of Mucic ended at 1.30 in the morning on 19th March, when he was transferred to the Police Detention Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: From the moment he was transferred to the police centre you know nothing about him, whether he was in a solitary confinement, whether he was detained with other prisoners, whether he complained of the treatment given to him, you know nothing more about it; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and there's no reason I should.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gschwendt. I have no further questions. Thank you, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Olujic. I think we had better start our 30 minutes' break here and come back at 12 for further cross-examination. (11.25 am). (Short break) (12.05 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Can we invite the witness so that we can continue with the cross-examination? (Witness re-entered court) (Interpreter re-entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Please remind him that he is on his oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that you are still testifying under oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You can carry on. May it please the court. Good afternoon, sir. My name is Tom Moran, and I am sure you have noticed I am one of the defence lawyers here. I am going to ask you a few questions and go through your direct examination this morning. It appeared to me from watching your direct examination that you speak some English; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Because of the interpretations here, what I say to you in English is going to be translated to you in German and at the same time it is going to be translated to other folks in French and Serbo-Croatian. Needless to say, this takes some time, so I know I have a habit of wanting to talk a little fast, and we're going to have to slow down for this. We are both going to have to make a conscious attempt to slow down. So will you do that with me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It's going to be as hard for me as it is for you. The other thing is if you don't understand a question I ask, will you stop me and tell me you don't understand? One other thing. You just nodded. There's a lady sitting up there named Melanie. She's the court reporter, and she's got to write down everything we say. She cannot write down a nod. So if we can say "yes" or "no", that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. First, back in March of 1996 you were part of the criminal police; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: KRIPO for short?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: By the way, I noticed you were testifying from some notes. In fact, you have them in front of you right now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: May I see them, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You want to examine his notes?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I would like to be able to know what he is testifying from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I don't know the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That's fine, your Honour. We will continue on then. I want to go over a few things with you. First, at the time Mr. Mucic was arrested it was, what, 18th March 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 18th March 1996, yes, about 2.15pm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And at the time you arrested him, you handed him a document known as information sheet for arrested persons, didn't you, or someone did, not you personally, but he was provided with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't testify to that. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. At some point -- I believe you testified during your direct that at some point during his incarceration with the Austrian criminal police that he was provided with a document known as information sheet for arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's a document that's prepared by the Austrian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And it reflects a person's rights under Austrian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, it's probably been checked over by your Justice Ministry to make sure that it truly and correctly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment on that, but I would assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You are familiar with that form, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's a one page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that form, to the best of your knowledge, truly and accurately reflects a suspect's rights while he is in custody under Austrian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not just that, but there's also the custody report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that has a lot of the same information, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For instance, whether one wants to consult a lawyer; whether one needs a doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, on your direct examination you were asked by Mr. Turone if anything was said to Mr. Mucic in an effort to induce him to speak to the Austrian police, were you not? You were asked that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was asked whether he wanted to testify and that he didn't have to testify if he would be incriminating himself thereby.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But, sir, the question that I asked and according to my notes you were asked: "Was anything said to Mr. Mucic in an effort to induce him to speak to the Austrian police?" Your answer was "no." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I hope he understands the question, that the question asked him during direct examination was whether anyone asked Mucic a question to induce him to make any statement, is what was asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a bit of misunderstanding there on my part. Nobody wanted to induce Mucic to make a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And you were also asked if anything was promised to him to get him to make a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I said that we couldn't promise him anything, because we had carried out the judge's arrest warrant and we had no influence on the further proceedings. So there weren't any promises we might have made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And, in fact, your answers included the phrase: "No, nothing was promised to Mr. Mucic", didn't it? Didn't your answer include that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Nothing was promised" -- nothing was promised to Mr. Mucic. That's quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: With the help of the usher I would like to send a document over to the witness, and the document is styled "Prosecution Response to Mucic Defence Motion to Exclude Evidence". I believe it is already in the court's file. I am going to ask him to refer to certain annexes to that. Sir, I am sure that you have probably never seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I've never seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Now attached to the back of the documents there are several documents which purport to be English translations of certain documents from the Austrian police, and I would direct your attention to annex number 3, way in the back. If it will help you, sir, up in the top in English it says "information sheet for arrested persons." It's there some place. You have found it? Take some time and if you need to talk to the interpreter sitting next to you, that's fine, go over that and see if that is a fair English translation of the document that's the standard document used by the Austrian police for an information sheet to arrested persons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With regard to the quality of what's written here, it's rather poor. I'm talking about the contents -- I am talking about the writing itself, rather. It's hard to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You mean it is a bad copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Your Honours, the defence lawyers were provided with the original German of this document. We made available the documents requested by Mr. Greaves on behalf of Mr. Mucic to all the defence lawyers with a letter dated, I believe, May -- I think 13th May -- 13th May -- 22nd May. So I don't think it's quite fair to invite the witness to be an interpreter in this room since his language is German.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: What he is saying is it is a poor translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with whether you sent the original to them. This is their own translation. Whether it is a good translation of the original German --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a translation prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor. It's not my translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Whoever did it, it is a translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: It is the Registrar's office which prepares translations anyway, not the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: It's not a reflection on you but what he says is it's a poor translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I don't have the original German. If the Prosecution has it there, I would be happy if they gave it to him. I am more interested in the content, not the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He said he has already given the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: You say it is a bad translation or it is a bad copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness did not say it was a bad translation; he said it was a bad copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now we've got that cleared up -- I thought that was correct -- is it readable, though? Can you read it and understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What would your question about this be?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to direct your attention to two paragraphs in that translation, specifically -- actually three, specifically 4, 5 and 7; okay? I'm going to read those out in English and I want to know if that is, in fact, the information, the advice given by the Austrian police to Mr. Mucic while he was in custody. Fair enough? If it was not the advice, let me know; okay? Paragraph number 4 starts off "presence of legal counsel"; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It says: "If you want your legal counsel to come and see you, as soon as possible make it known". It continues on: "You may not have legal counsel present when you are questioned for a criminal offence". Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It continues on: "In that case, therefore, you will have an opportunity to see and speak to your lawyer only after you have been questioned, but even then only if it has been determined that you will be transferred to the court prison and there is sufficient time remaining until then"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: It further goes on: "Such consultation with your lawyer will, moreover, only be considered if there is no risk of prejudicing the course of justice". That's what it says, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means -- this whole article means that the person has the right to consult a lawyer, but that the lawyer cannot be present during the questioning and there's also the matter of the time availability, and that consultation with a lawyer may only take place if there is no possibility of that impeding the procedure, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What does it mean by -- who decides whether a consultation between a person charged with a criminal offence and his attorney has a risk of prejudicing the course of justice? Do you decide that as a KRIPO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this case we would have a legal expert, an officer who's got a legal background there, and it would be he who would take that kind of decision, but in this case it was not required, because Mr. Mucic did not want a lawyer, which he confirmed several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But the decision of whether or not this person is going to be allowed to consult with an attorney, any person that's arrested, me, you, anyone who's arrested, the decision of whether or not he's going to be allowed to consult with counsel prior to questioning is a determination made by the criminal police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I thought I had said that there's an officer who is a legal expert and he would take that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Is he part of the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He's part of the police, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So the police make the decision on whether or not a suspect in custody, me, for instance, has the right to consult with a lawyer prior to any questioning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this instance, in this specific instance --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'd like to refer to this case. I don't want to give you general legal information.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm going over this information sheet that was given to Mr. Mucic by a representative of the Austrian criminal police and help me -- if I could ask the questions, if the Prosecution thinks there's some confusion they have the right to come back and ask you more questions. I'm simply asking you about the information that was given to Mr. Mucic, not about this case. I'm asking about information; okay? Can we do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much?.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now let's get what you really want as a matter of general practice, is it, or, as he is inferring, in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going into the information and advice that was given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is general information for every case which comes before the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So that is what you are asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, just what is on the sheet and what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Now the second thing is if I am a suspect in custody or anyone is a suspect in custody, they do not have the right to have their lawyer sitting next to them while they are being questioned by the police, do they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The suspect has no right to have the lawyer with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that's because if I were sitting next to a client who was being questioned by you, I might tell him to stop answering your questions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Austrian law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. So let's see if I can sum up what Austrian law is as it applies to the presence of legal counsel during questioning by the police, and tell me if this is a fair assessment of both Austrian law and the advice that was given to Mr. Mucic; okay? If I'm wrong, stop me. That a suspect in custody, be it Pavo Mucic or Tom Moran or anyone else, has the right to call a lawyer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: But the Austrian police, someone in the police makes the decision about whether or not that person can talk to a lawyer prior to questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And that even if that suspect who is in custody is allowed to talk to a lawyer, if the Austrian police allow them to, they have to be questioned alone without the help of their lawyer there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, but I would like to stress again in this case it wasn't relevant, because Mr. Mucic said several times that he did not want a lawyer, and he also signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And he did all of that after you handed him an information sheet that said: "You can't talk to the lawyer unless we say it's okay, and even if you talk to the lawyer, he can't be with you while we're questioning you"; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's Austrian law. You can't blame me for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: What counsel is saying is he signed whatever he did after reading the instructions which you handed over to him that he could not have his counsel by him during questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on to paragraph 5; okay? It says: "Counsel or representation. If you are a foreigner you have a right to request that the counsel representative of your home country be informed of your arrest"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and Mr. Mucic did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No question about it, and the question I'm going to ask you, and you may not know the answer, is: do you know what law requires that warning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not know the specific law.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So if I told you that it were required by the Vienna Convention on Counsellor Relations of 1962, you wouldn't quarrel with me, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Let's go on to paragraph Number 7. Take some time if you want to read it and then we'll go over it the same way we did paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine. Let's go to the first paragraph -- the first sentence. It says: "You will have the opportunity to speak about the accusations against you". The next sentence says: "If you do not use it and remain silent instead, you are depriving yourself of the possibility to give an account of things from your perspective and to defend yourself". Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: What does that mean? What does that mean to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that the individual has the possibility to speak about the accusations from his or her point of view, and if the person decides to remain silent, that the person is depriving him or herself of that possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, if I choose to remain silent during an interview where I'm a suspect in custody, how am I deprived of the opportunity to defend myself? Does that mean that my right to present evidence of my side of the story is gone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It doesn't mean that you've lost your right, rather if, for instance, you have a valid alibi and you remain silent, then the police can't check ought that alibi and that alibi could mean that you would released immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: That's the next sentence, is it not? It says: "Your statements may also help clear up a mistake". That's the next sentence in that paragraph, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Then it continues: "You need not speak about the case. However, in the event of a sentence, if you confess or otherwise contribute through your statement to" -- what is that -- "deciding the truth, indicating the truth"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Elucidating".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: "Elucidating the truth, it will be taken into consideration as grounds for mitigation". Isn't that what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you repeat that last word?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sure. I will repeat the whole sentence for you, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay: "You need not speak about the case. However, in the event of a sentence, if you confess or otherwise contribute through your statement to elucidating the truth, it will be taken into consideration as grounds for mitigation".

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Maybe it would be more fair for the witness to have anyway the German original in his hands, if he prefers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Fine with me. If you have a copy of it, let him have it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there were a German copy, that would be nice. (Handed). Thank you. I've read it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. What I said in English is a fair translation of what is in the document that was given to Pavo Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And other -- every other suspect who's arrested by the Austrian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everyone gets this, question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: You said there was no threats or promises that were made to him to get him to talk; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So you don't consider telling a person: "If you don't talk now you're going to lose the right to defend yourself, but if you do talk and you get sentenced you are going to get a lighter sentence" not to be an inducement to talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not the way it's stated here, the way you've put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Well, we've just been over it, and that's exactly what it says?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't share that point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So it doesn't say that if you're found guilty and you confess, it will be taken into account as grounds for mitigation? It doesn't say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour. This is arguing between defence lawyer and the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think they are trying to elucidate that portion of the instruction. It doesn't make any difference. It's not arguing with him. It's merely telling him what that portion means more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Let me try it this way. What does the word "mitigation" mean to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the interpreter might make one comment, the German word is "Milderungsgrund".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Code of Criminal Procedure it says that a confession is grounds for mitigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So this accurately reflects Austrian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Now let's try again. The word mitigation or what the interpreter said is the German word, what does that mean as a practical matter? Does it mean that the judge, when he sentences you, will say: "Well, I'm going to give you life in prison but I sure feel bad about it and I wish you the best of luck" or does it mean the judge says: "Rather than giving you life in the penitentiary, I am going to give you five years in mitigation"? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A confession is in general terms a grounds for mitigation, just as there are other grounds for mitigation. If somebody has done something under coercion, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So as a ground for mitigation if you give a confession when the police ask you for one, the hope is there and, in fact, the law provides that that should be something to reduce your punishment; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what's provided for under the law, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you wouldn't call that an inducement to talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't see it that way. It's drawing his attention to some legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: No question about it. I'm not telling you it's not the provision of your law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not a promise. It's not a promise that's being made by the police. This is a statement of the Austrian legal situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And it was a statement of the Austrian legal situation that was given to Pavo Mucic before Pavo made a statement to the KRIPOS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It's part of his rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And he understood what you told him, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Supput, the interpreter, translated it to him and I assume he understood it. I wouldn't sign anything that I hadn't understood.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: So we can all agree when Pavo Mucic agreed to talk to you, he was well aware of the import to giving a statement to the police; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I share that view.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, he was taken before a magistrate, Dr Seda, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Would Dr Seda have given Mr. Mucic the same advice that is contained in this advice sheet we have been talking about, the information sheet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. There are no police officers present before the investigating magistrate. As I already said, on the 19th at 1.30 in the morning the police dealings with Mr. Mucic came to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. During your questioning of -- not yours but of the Austrian police officers' questioning of Mr. Mucic, there was some considerable detail in the questions about what Mr. Mucic was charged with, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was the charge, the accusations that were clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: In fact, you'd been briefed by members of the Office of the Prosecutor from this Tribunal on the kinds of questions to ask, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. You met with some investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And you had a long discussion with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not very long. It was already midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, and they talked to you about the case, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As best as I recall, we talked merely about the further proceedings, their contacts with the Ministry of Justice and their contacts with Interpol, but as regards to the details, I can't remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay, but clearly -- did they ask you to take a statement from Mr. Mucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say, but when someone is arrested, when someone is taken into custody, the procedure is that you have this questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Even when he's not charged with anything under Austrian law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was an Austrian arrest warrant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: And the Austrian arrest warrant was a warrant -- well, that package of papers in front of you, turn to annex 1. If it will help you, it is the page right behind all the signatures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I don't think you have it. Keep going. It's behind all of the signatures. It's annex 1. It's a copy of the arrest warrant is what it is: the first words on the top of the page in all capital letters are "warrant of arrest"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. That warrant of arrest, take a look at it, says that he was arrested to secure his extradition to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, isn't that right. It doesn't say anything about him being charged with any offence against Austrian law, does it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's try it again. Is it the policy and the habit of the Austrian Police Department -- let me give you a hypothetical example. Suppose that I were indicted by a Federal Grand Jury in the United States for an offence -- pick an offence -- obstructing justice -- and I were found in Vienna, and the Federal Bureau of Investigation through Interpol asked you to arrest me and put me on an aeroplane and send me back to the United States to answer these charges, you would get a warrant for my arrest from an Austrian magistrate, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's a question which really is too legal for me. I'm in charge of executing things, not for judgments of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Okay. At some point if you knew where I was and the Federal Bureau of Investigation asked you to arrest me, you would send some of your officers out to arrest me, wouldn't you, following whatever procedures are used by the criminal police in Austria to arrest people for extradition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you state that question in different terms?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Sure.
